title: Interop playbook: TRT + Triton + KV cache + scheduler
content:
Purpose:
This document is a lightweight playbook and design note for integrating TensorRT (TRT), Triton, and our custom kernels into the Redwood serving runtime with an emphasis on KV cache placement and scheduler policies. It collects tradeoffs observed in early prototypes, proposes a small experiment matrix, and sketches a rollout plan for production-safe adoption.

Background and motivation:
- TRT can deliver large per-token throughput gains for decoder-only transformer blocks when kernels map cleanly to its supported ops and when optimization profiles are well-defined.
- Triton (server) provides model packaging, dynamic routing, and multi-backend support. It simplifies fallbacks and routing logic but can add RPC and process isolation overhead.
- Custom kernels (CUDA extensions) allow us to implement ops or fused paths (attention with rotary, complex kv-copy patterns) that neither TRT nor Triton covers efficiently.
- KV cache placement (GPU-resident, pinned host memory, or split) materially affects latency tail and memory footprint.
- Scheduler policies (latency-first, throughput-first, hybrid) must be tuned based on customer SLOs and cost targets.

Goals:
1) Define safe integration modes that maximize throughput while preserving latency SLOs and correctness.
2) Provide a reproducible experiment matrix and instrumentation plan.
3) Produce a rollout checklist for Canary -> Dedicated -> General availability.

Constraints and invariants:
- Correctness first: fallbacks must preserve numerics and sequence continuity for KV cache.
- Memory caps per GPU are limited; larger contexts require eviction policies or multi-GPU chaining.
- TRT requires static-ish optimization profiles for max_batch x max_seq; dynamic shapes reduce TRT efficacy.
- Some ops (e.g., certain custom tokenizers, exotic rotary variants) are not supported in TRT and must be handled by Triton/custom kernels.

Integration modes (high level):
A) Single-process TRT runtime: embed TRT engine into our serving runtime (no Triton) using an adapter layer.
   - Pros: lowest intra-request overhead, tight control over batching and KV layout, easiest zero-copy GPU KV cache.
   - Cons: more maintenance, implementing model packaging and fallback logic ourselves.

B) Triton-managed models with TRT backend + sidecar custom kernels: Triton hosts TRT engines, sidecar handles custom ops and unified KV cache via IPC.
   - Pros: modular, easier model lifecycle, native Triton monitoring, facilitates mixed-backend fallbacks.
   - Cons: additional RPC/IPC overhead, more latency variance, complexity in ensuring zero-copy for KV.

C) Hybrid: primary inference path in TRT (embedded or Triton), with on-path fallthrough to our custom CUDA kernels for unsupported ops, sharing KV via GPU-resident buffers exported across runtimes (CUDA IPC or shared CUDA memory).
   - Pros: best performance when most ops supported by TRT; flexible fallback.
   - Cons: requires robust CUDA IPC bookkeeping and cold-start warmup logic.

KV cache placement options and tradeoffs:
1) GPU-resident (single-GPU): fastest token latency, cheapest for hot prefixes, but limited by per-GPU memory. Scaling to large context sizes requires multi-GPU strategies.
2) Pinned host memory (page-locked): lower GPU memory usage, modest copy overhead per new KV fetch, predictable when GPU memory is exhausted. Good for bursty workloads if combined with local caching.
3) Split KV (recent tokens GPU, older context pinned-host or remote): complex eviction policy, requires application-visible consistency guarantees for attention keys. Helps support very large contexts with bounded GPU footprint.

Eviction and warming heuristics:
- LRU over prefix chunks (e.g., 128-token window) with async prefetch for predicted next tokens (based on request pattern).
- Warmup on model load: pre-run a short batch to populate TRT engine workspace and prebuild CUDA graph/kernels; pre-allocate KV buffers to reduce later allocation stalls.
- Sticky-connection affinity: affinity-based scheduling for hot clients to keep KV cache warm on the same GPU.

Scheduler policies (design sketches):
1) Latency-first (SLA): small target batch sizes, immediate dispatch, aggressive preemption of long-running batches; prefer GPU-resident KV.
2) Throughput-first (cost-sensitive): allow larger batching windows, multiplex clients into batches, tolerate slightly higher tail latencies; favor Triton scheduling if it gives better packing.
3) Hybrid adaptive: monitor per-route tail latency and adjust batching_window and batcher_lookback dynamically; if tail exceeds threshold, switch batcher to latency mode.

Kernel compatibility layer (KCL):
- Purpose: present a unified op interface to the serving runtime so we can route subgraphs to TRT, Triton CPU, or custom kernels without changing higher-level routing logic.
- Minimal API surface: init(engine_profile), run(inputs, kv_handles), async_run(...), serialize_state().
- Fallback semantics: deterministic fallback order with metric tagging (e.g., trt:success, trt:partial, custom:used).

Experiment matrix (suggested):
- Variables:
  * Model family: decoder-small(1B), decoder-med(7B), decoder-large(70B) (use reduced batch/seq for large models)
  * Integration mode: A, B, C (see above)
  * KV placement: GPU, pinned-host, split
  * Scheduler: latency-first, throughput-first, hybrid
  * Quantization level: FP16, INT8 (post-training calibration)
- Metrics to capture per run:
  * p50/p95/p99 latency (token and request), tokens/sec, GPU utilization, memcpy bandwidth, memory foot print, failure/retry rate, tail jitter.
- Small sample table (synthetic runs):
  * decoder-med, TRT embedded, GPU KV, latency-first -> p50 token: 12ms, p95: 28ms, tokens/sec: 1200, gpu%: 68
  * decoder-med, Triton TRT backend + sidecar, pinned-host KV, throughput-first -> p50 token: 18ms, p95: 46ms, tokens/sec: 1600, gpu%: 84, memcpy overhead visible
  * decoder-large, hybrid, split KV, hybrid scheduler -> p50 token: 55ms, p95: 140ms, tokens/sec: 350, memory pressure reduced by 30%
(These numbers are illustrative; exact numbers to be captured by experiments.)

Instrumentation and observability:
- Tag traces with chosen backend, kernel version, optimization profile id, and KV placement.
- Expose counters for kernel fallbacks, memcpy sizes, CUDA IPC serialization events, and KV eviction counts.
- Per-route SLO evaluations and automatic rollback triggers if p95 increases > 20% after rollout.

Rollout plan (canary -> dedicated -> GA):
1) Canary (internal traffic): run mode C (hybrid) with GPU-resident KV on small set of nodes; collect traces and mismatch logs vs Triton-only baseline.
2) Limited external beta: enable Triton-managed TRT backend with pinned-host KV for customers who opt-in; monitor cost and latency.
3) Dedicated GA: allow customers to pin integration mode, provide runbooks for KV sizing and scheduler presets (latency vs throughput).

Risks and mitigations:
- TRT model mismatch (unsupported op) -> detect at model onboarding and generate auto-fallback graph split. Coverage tests in onboarding pipeline.
- CUDA IPC fragility across kernel versions -> pin driver/CUDA minor versions per release, add runtime compatibility checks.
- Memory fragmentation due to dynamic allocation -> pre-allocate pools and use arena allocators.

Open questions (todo / decision points):
- Should we standardize on a single canonical IPC mechanism for KV (CUDA IPC vs NVSHMEM vs RDMA) for all deployments? (Action: prototype NVSHMEM for split-KV)
- How aggressive should the scheduler be about preemption when mixing long-generation jobs and short chat-style queries?
- Best approach to represent dynamic shapes to TRT when sequence length varies widely across requests while still retaining TRT performance.

Next steps and owners:
- Run controlled experiment matrix for decoder-med with the three integration modes (owner: Marcus, ETA: 2 weeks).
- Prototype NVSHMEM-backed shared KV for split strategy (owner: Ravi, ETA: 3 weeks).
- Add KCL shim and metric tags in tracing (owner: Ellen, ETA: 1 week).
- Write onboarding checks that fail model promos when required TRT ops are missing (owner: Aisha, ETA: 2 weeks).

Appendix: quick checklist for a single new model onboarding to TRT path
- Verify model graph ops against TRT plugin compatibility list.
- Generate candidate optimization profiles for expected batch/seq combos.
- Run small synthetic bench for warmup and cold-start latency.
- Validate KV cache warmup behavior with a 500-request replay from production trace.
- If fallback needed, produce a deterministic split plan (which subgraphs run in TRT vs custom).

Notes to self (rough):
- Investigate kernel-level fused rotary+scale + kv-append operator that could be a high ROI for int8 quantized decoders.
- Consider an experimental endpoint flag to force pinned-host KV for debugging memory pressure issues.

References:
- GH#4821: triton-trt-fallback-protos (PR draft)
- JIRA-INF-204: KV-cache-eviction-policy
- confluence/serving-runtime/kvcache-playbook (shared reference)

End of draft.
